_comment: Devin CLI permission policy for benchmark runs. The harness copies this to
<workspace>/.devin/config.json for every run (see BenchConfig.devin_permissions_file).
Why it exists: Devin's non-interactive (-p) mode cannot prompt, so it silently
rejects any tool call needing approval. This policy pre-approves exactly the
workspace edits and build/test commands a coding task needs, instead of using
--permission-mode dangerous, which would auto-approve everything.
Semantics (verified against the CLI):
* deny beats allow.
* Exec() matches a command prefix on whole-word boundaries: Exec(git) matches
'git status' but not 'gitk'.
* Compound commands are checked per segment: with Exec(cd) allowed and
Exec(wget) denied, 'cd /tmp && wget ...' is still denied.
* Exec() takes literal prefixes only — NO globs. Exec(*/bin/python) and
Exec(**/bin/pip) both fail to match, so an interpreter invoked by path
must be listed verbatim (see the venv entries below).
Why the shell is ALLOWED here, and what that costs:
A command allowlist cannot be both airtight and complete across a
heterogeneous task suite. Denying bash/sh made real runs fail in ways that
measured the policy instead of the CLI: bedrock-sentiment died having
written nothing because 'which sam; sam --version; ...' hit one unlisted
segment, and dashboard could not write its own scratch test because that
used a heredoc. A rejection aborts the run at exit code 0, so the harness
scores it as a failure — silently turning a policy gap into 'Devin is
worse', which is exactly the unfairness this benchmark must avoid.
Allowing the shell means the Exec deny list below is best-effort, not a
boundary: 'bash -c "<denied cmd>"' runs because the inner command is only
an argument. The deny entries are kept as a speed bump against the direct
invocation, not as containment.
curl/wget are therefore ALLOWED rather than denied. Denying them bought no
security once the shell was allowed, but it did cost a real measurement:
harden-k8s scored 15% having written nothing, because Devin tried to look
up a pinned image tag with curl, was refused, and stopped. Kiro and Claude
Code run the same task with --trust-all-tools and
--dangerously-skip-permissions, so both had network access and both scored
100%. A deny that only binds the runner being measured produces a fake
capability gap, which is the specific failure mode this benchmark exists to
avoid. Egress restriction, if wanted, has to come from the sandbox or the
network layer and be applied to all three runners equally.
Containment comes from the workspace instead. Each run gets a fresh
disposable directory (see Workspace in agent_cost_bench/sandbox.py), and the
other two runners already run with --trust-all-tools and
--dangerously-skip-permissions, so this puts all three CLIs on comparable
footing. Devin's --sandbox flag would enforce Read/Write scopes at the OS
level (macOS seatbelt) and is the better model, but it requires autonomous
mode, which an organization policy can restrict; re-test it before relying
on it.
Do NOT run this suite against a workspace_base holding anything you care
about, and do not treat the deny list as protecting the host.
Adding a command: put Exec(<command>) in allow. An unlisted command is
rejected, not prompted, so a task needing it will fail rather than hang.
